title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (4 of 7)
hook: it moves and it does not move; it is far, and it is near
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma; don't let the work stick, and keep working. Doing works here, one may wish to live a hundred years, and the action doesn't cling. Did you wash your hands of one job? Day two hundred thirty-five.

Try describing the sky to someone. It's up there. But it's also right here, touching your face; you're breathing it. It's the biggest thing you'll ever see and you can't hold a piece of it. Every sentence you make about it is true and a little wrong. Verses four and five of the Isha try to describe the one who pervades all this. And instead of a definition, they give you a string of contradictions. On purpose.
screen: `DESCRIBE THE SKY.` → `TRUE, AND A LITTLE WRONG.` → `A STRING OF CONTRADICTIONS.`

segments.voice: Verse four: it is one, unmoving, and swifter than the mind. The senses can't catch it; it's always ahead of them. Standing still, it outruns those who run. Then verse five: tad ejati tan naijati. It moves; it does not move. Tad dure tad v antike. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and it is outside all this. Why talk like this? Because any single statement would shrink it. Say it's far away, in heaven, and you've made it absent from your kitchen. Say it's right here, and you've made it small enough to fit in a room. The Upanishad holds both at once, the way you'd hold two ends of a rope to keep it taut. It's the same move you met in the Gita, where Krishna says everything rests in him and also that he isn't contained by any of it. Different schools of Hindu thought later read these verses differently. Those who follow Shankara's Advaita, non-duality, hear the one reality behind every appearance. Those who follow Ramanuja hear a personal Lord who lives in everything as its inner self, while still being more than it. Both are reading the same two lines. And notice where this sits: right after the verses about living and working in the world. The one you're looking for is not only at the end of a long journey. It's also near, nearer than the next thought. Swifter than the mind, and still.
screen: `SWIFTER THAN THE MIND.` · `IT MOVES; IT DOES NOT MOVE.` · `FAR, AND NEAR.` · `INSIDE ALL THIS, AND OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `TAD DURE TAD V ANTIKE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit very still. Notice that even while your body is still, something moves: the breath, the heartbeat, a thought passing. Stillness and movement, both at once. Now notice something far away: a sound outside, the thought of someone in another city. Then something near: the air on your skin. Let the verse sit with you: it moves, it does not move; far, and near. You don't have to understand it. Just notice both. The bell holds the time.
Ejati, it moves, it stirs. Tad ejati tan naijati: it moves, it does not move; it is far, and it is near, inside all this and outside it.
Your line: nearer than the next thought. Today, catch one moment when you're looking far away for something, and check what's near. Day two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Isha verse 5, 'tad ejati tan naijati', is chanted in Vedic recitation and quoted in Hindu teaching to show that the divine is both beyond the world and within it.

myth: the Isha describes the one behind all this with a single clear definition
it gives contradictions on purpose: it moves and doesn't move, far and near.
verse four says it outruns those who run while standing still
unmoving, swifter than the mind; the senses never catch it.
every Hindu school reads these verses the same way
Advaita hears one reality; Ramanuja's school hears a personal Lord indwelling all.

fork.setup: you want to describe the one who pervades all this. what do you say?
options: it lives far away, in heaven.
it is right here, in this room, and nowhere else.
it moves and doesn't move; far, and near.
fork.reveal: the Isha refuses to shrink it: inside all this and outside it, at once.

original.note: Sanskrit: ejati, it moves, it stirs; verse five: tad ejati tan naijati, it moves, it does not move.

trapdoor: what you thought: contradictions mean the text is confused.
what it means: holding both sides keeps the divine from being made too far or too small.
what a scholar hears: verses 4–5 use paired opposites (ejati/naijati, dure/antike, antar/bahya), a style the Gita echoes in chapter 13.
